title: Wholesale versus retail on one domain
metaTitle: Wholesale and retail need two doors
excerpt: Give wholesale its own path, prices, and account rules on the same domain. A toggle on a consumer product page makes the shopper and the trade buyer guess which rules apply.
alt: A white geometric building with a glass wing and a cantilevered upper volume. Two volumes on one structure, the way retail and wholesale can share a domain.
caption: One building, two distinct volumes. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Can wholesale and retail share a domain?
faqs.answer: Yes, if each buyer has a front door, a set of rules, and templates that do not swap underneath them. Shared type and photography are fine. A shared cart, a shared price, or a switch on the consumer product page mixes two businesses.

faqs.question: When should trade prices be visible?
faqs.answer: Show them after you have stated the minimum, the region, and the payment terms, and only to people who are allowed to order that way. A guest who can see a case price will either try to buy one unit or think the retail price is a penalty.

faqs.question: What if wholesale is not ready?
faqs.answer: Do not leave a wholesale link that ends in an error or a password with no explanation. A labeled sentence and a real application, even a short one, is a more honest door. Add the catalog when you can fulfill the rules you publish.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A wholesale and retail website can live on one domain only if the two buyers never have to guess which rules they are under. Give wholesale its own path, its own prices, and its own account rules. A toggle on a consumer product page asks both people to do work that belongs to the shop.

The retail buyer wants the object, the price, and a way to purchase today. The wholesale buyer wants terms, minimums, and a way to reorder without pretending to be a guest. Those are different jobs. One shared grid with a switch on top usually serves neither.

## Two buyers, two front doors

People decide quickly whether a page is for them. Nielsen Norman Group’s 2011 article on [how long users stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) notes that users often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and that a clear value proposition in the first 10 seconds is what holds them. A homepage that says “shop” and “wholesale” in the same breath, with no clue which click is theirs, spends that window on a choice you could have made in the navigation.

Put retail at the main path. It is the public shop: prices, shipping, a bag. Put wholesale behind a labeled path: “Wholesale” in the header, leading to a page that says who it is for, what the minimum is, and how to apply or sign in. Do not make a consumer click “retail” to escape a trade view they never asked for.

The first screen of each path should be readable by a stranger in that role. Retail opens on the collection. Wholesale opens on the terms and the catalog they are allowed to see. If a buyer can land on the wrong one from an ad, the page they land on should say, in a sentence, where the other door is. That sentence is a courtesy. It is not a toggle that rewrites the product.

Write the nav labels in the words your buyers use. “Trade” means something in some industries and nothing in others. “Stockists” is right for some brands and opaque for a first-time buyer. Pick the word you already say on the phone, and use it in the header, the title, and the application.

## What wholesale is allowed to show

Wholesale prices are not a skin on the retail price. They come with conditions: a minimum order, a case pack, a region, a lead time, net-30 or pay now. Show those conditions before you show a number, or show them in the same block as the number. A price with no minimum is an invitation for a one-unit order you cannot fulfill, or for a consumer who thinks they found a secret discount.

Require an approved account before trade prices appear if the prices are not public. The application can be short: business name, resale evidence you actually check, region, and what they intend to carry. Say how long a decision takes, in a window you keep. “We reply within three business days” is a window. “We’ll be in touch” is how applications rot in a mailbox.

Once they are in, the catalog should be the trade catalog. Case quantities, available dates, and the line sheet as a file they can send to their own buyer. Retail storytelling can be a link. It should not be the only way to see a SKU. A buyer writing an order on a Tuesday does not want a lookbook between them and the size run.

Keep retail customers out of that catalog by accident. Shared carts, shared wishlists, and a “view as” switch that sticks in the browser are how a consumer checks out at a trade price or a buyer sees a consumer promotion that does not apply. Separate sessions. If you must preview, make the preview obvious and temporary.

## What retail must not inherit

The consumer product page should not mention nets, line sheets, or “login for trade price” as the primary action. A small text link, “Are you a stockist?”, can sit in the footer of the page and go to the wholesale door. The purchase path stays a purchase path.

Do not show two prices to a guest. Crossed-out trade numbers, member teasers, and “from” prices that are really case prices make the retail price look like a penalty. If the retail price is the real price for this visitor, it is the only price on the page.

Promotions should be explicit about which door they use. A sample sale for consumers and a forward-order discount for trade will get mixed in a shared banner. Put the banner on the path it belongs to. A sitewide strip is how the wrong person claims the wrong offer, and then your inbox spends a day unwinding it.

Inventory language differs too. Retail can say what is in the warehouse now. Wholesale often needs what will be cut, what is already allocated, and what the reorder date is. Using “in stock” for both will create orders you cannot ship under the promise the buyer heard.

## Accounts, tax, and the order itself

A wholesale account is a record: company, buyers allowed to order, shipping addresses, tax exemption on file, payment terms. Build the minimum that your operations will actually check. A ten-field application you never read is theater. Ask for the document you require, and say what happens if it is missing.

Tax and shipping rules should follow the account, not a code the buyer types at the end. If they are exempt, the bag should already know. If they must ship to a store address, do not offer a home-address shortcut that creates a second set of books.

The order confirmation should read like a trade document when it is a trade order: PO number if you accept one, ship window, payment due date, and the person to reply to. The retail receipt can stay lighter. One template with the wrong nouns is how a stockist feels like an afterthought.

Reorders are the point of the account. Let an approved buyer repeat a past order and change quantities without rebuilding the case from a consumer grid. If the line has changed, say what was discontinued. Do not silently substitute.

## A domain can still be one brand

One domain is reasonable. The brand is one brand. The logo, the type, and the photography can be shared so a stockist and a customer recognize the same house. Sharing a visual system is not the same as sharing a checkout.

Use a clear path in the URL if it helps your team, such as a wholesale section with its own templates. What matters is that the templates do not swap under a visitor who did not ask. A control that says “shop as wholesale” on a product the consumer is midway through buying will be clicked by curiosity, and then the bag will be wrong.

Search should send each query to the right door. A retail campaign should not land on a login wall. A trade ad should not land on a consumer sale. Check the titles. A page title that says only the brand name forces both buyers to open the page to learn which room it is.

If you are not ready to serve trade on the site, do not leave a wholesale link that 404s or dumps into a password with no explanation. A sentence and an email path, clearly labeled, is a more honest door than a broken one. When you are ready, replace the sentence with the real application.

Down the Cove’s public work is an ecommerce migration and redesign, the retail shape of a shop. Wholesale, if you add it later, should be scoped as its own path rather than a mode flag on those product templates. The cost of a flag is the confused orders. The cost of a path is a second set of templates you can explain.

## How to tell the toggle is already hurting

Read the last month of orders and the last month of support mail. The pattern is usually obvious once you look.

- Consumers asking why a price changed after login
- Trade buyers sending screenshots of the retail page because they cannot find the line sheet
- Orders for a single unit at a case price
- A banner offer claimed by the wrong group

If you see those, remove the switch from the consumer product page first. Send wholesale to its own front door, even if the first version of that door is a short application and a PDF line sheet. A clear split with a plain tool beats a clever toggle that mixes the bags. You can rebuild the trade catalog in the site once the rules are stable. Do not wait for a perfect portal before you stop showing two prices to a guest.

The public face of a brand is often a lookbook, and that surface has a different job again. [A lookbook that still leads to a product](/blog/a-lookbook-that-still-leads-to-a-product) is the next read if your story pages are starting to replace the shop, for retail or for the buyers you are trying to win.

If both doors are in scope and you want a second pair of eyes on which templates you actually need, [book an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the two buyers and the rules each one must see. The call is for sorting the paths, not for picking a theme.
